topicTitle: Angiosperm: morphology of root, stem, leaves, inflorescences, flowers and fruit; taxonomic study: definition, taxonomic hierarchy, classification systems (artificial, natural and phylogenetic) of angiosperms; angiosperm families with economic importance: Brassicaceae, Fabaceae, Solanaceae and Liliaceae
notes: **Root types:** tap root (dicots, from radicle) and adventitious/fibrous root (monocots, from stem base). Modified roots: tuber, aerial, prop, pneumatophore.
**Stem modifications:** runner, rhizome, corm, tuber, bulb, sucker, stolon, thorn, spine, cladode.
**Leaf types:** simple vs compound, phyllotaxy (alternate, opposite, whorled), venation ( reticulate in dicots, parallel in monocots).
**Inflorescence:** racemose (indeterminate: raceme, spike, panicle, spadix) vs cymose (determinate: monochasial, dichasial).
**Flower parts:** calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens: filament + anther), gynoecium (carpels: stigma + style + ovary).
**Fruit types:** fleshy (berry, drupe, pome) and dry (dehiscent: legume, follicle, capsule; indehiscent: achene, caryopsis, nut).
**Classification systems:** artificial (Linnaeus, sexual system), natural (Bentham and Hooker, Engler and Prantl), phylogenetic (APG, molecular DNA-based).

**Economic families:** Brassicaceae (mustard, cruciferae, tetradynamous), Fabaceae (legumes, nitrogen fixers, papilionaceous), Solanaceae (potato, tomato, nightshade), Liliaceae (onion, garlic, tulip).

**Angiosperm advantages over gymnosperms:** enclosed seeds (ovary protects ovule → fruit protects seed), double fertilisation (efficient nutritive tissue formation), vessel elements in xylem (more efficient water transport), flowers attract pollinators (higher fertilisation success).
**Flower symmetry:** actinomorphic (radially symmetrical, e.g., mustard, Datura) vs zygomorphic (bilaterally symmetrical, e.g., pea, orchid) vs asymmetrical (e.g., Canna).
**Ovary position:** hypogynous (ovary superior, e.g., mustard), perigynous (ovary half-inferior, floral cup surrounds it, e.g., rose), epigynous (ovary inferior, e.g., apple, sunflower).

**Placenta types:** marginal (Fabaceae — ovules on ridge of bilocular ovary), axile (mustard, lemon — ovules on central axis), basal (Sunflower — single ovule at base), free central (Primrose — ovules on central column, septa absent), parietal (mustard family some members — ovules on ovary wall).
**Monocot vs Dicot flower:** monocot flowers typically trimerous (3 parts), dicot flowers typically tetramerous/pentamerous (4 or 5 parts). This is a reliable diagnostic feature.

**Bentham & Hooker classification:** Natural system based on floral characters. Divided into 3 subclasses: Polypetalae (free petals), Gamopetalae (fused petals), Monochlamydeae (perianth absent or undifferentiated). Included gymnosperms separately.

**APG system:** Angiosperm Phylogeny Group, based on molecular data (chloroplast genes, nuclear rRNA). Divides angiosperms into: basal angiosperms (Amborella, water lilies, magnolias), monocots, and eudicots (true dicots) + asterids + rosids. Currently the most accepted system.

**Brassicaceae family key features:** 4 sepals, 4 petals (cruciform/cross-shaped arrangement), 6 stamens (4 long + 2 short = tetradynamous), superior ovary, fruit is silique or silicle. Examples: Brassica, Mustard, Radish.

**Fabaceae family key features:** papilionaceous corolla (banner, 2 wings, keel), diadelphous stamens (9+1), superior ovary, fruit is legume (pod). Sub-family Papilionoideae has this distinctive flower. Nitrogen fixation via Rhizobium symbiosis in root nodules.

**Solanaceae family key features:** 5 fused sepals, 5 fused petals (gamopetalous), 5 stamens (epipetalous — attached to petals), superior ovary, fruit is berry or capsule. Many alkaloids (nicotine, solanine, atropine). Examples: Potato, Tomato, Tobacco, Brinjal.

**Liliaceae family key features:** 6 tepals (undifferentiated calyx and corolla), 6 stamens, superior ovary, trimerous flowers, fruit is capsule or berry. Examples: Lily, Allium (onion, garlic), Aloe.

**Taxonomic hierarchy:** Species < Genus < Family < Order < Class < Division/Phylum < Kingdom. Binomial nomenclature (Genus + species epithet) is standard. Author citation follows the name (e.g., Mangifera indica L.).

**Inflorescence types — detailed:** Racemose: raceme (elongated axis, flowers on pedicels, e.g., Mustard), spike (sessile flowers, e.g., Amaranthus), spikelet (small spike, grasses), catkin (pendulous, e.g., Betula), spadix (fleshy axis, e.g., Coconut, Colocasia), capitulum/cyathium (head, e.g., Sunflower, Euphorbia). Cymose: monochasial (scorpioid, helicoid, e.g., Solanum), dichasial (e.g., Dianthus).

**Flower formula symbols:** K = calyx (from German Kelch), C = corolla (from Latin Corolla), A = androecium, G = gynoecium. Numbers in brackets indicate fused parts (e.g., C(5) = 5 fused petals). Placing G with a line underneath = superior ovary; line above = inferior ovary.

**Double fertilisation process:** In angiosperms, one sperm fuses with the egg to form the zygote (2n) — syngamy. The other sperm fuses with two polar nuclei (or a secondary nucleus) to form the primary endosperm nucleus (3n) — triple fusion. The result is a zygote + triploid endosperm. This is UNIQUE to angiosperms.

**Parietal vs axile placentation:** In parietal placentation, ovules are on the inner wall of a unilocular ovary (e.g., Papaver). In axile placentation, ovules are on a central axis in a multi-locular ovary (e.g., Solanum, Citrus). The distinction is important for fruit classification.

**Perianth terminology:** When calyx and corolla are distinct, they are called sepal and petal respectively. When indistinguishable, the term 'tepals' is used (common in monocots like Liliaceae, monocots generally). Monochlamydeous flowers have only one whorl of perianth (tepals) or none.

**True fruit vs false fruit:** True fruit develops only from the ovary (e.g., mango, tomato). False fruit (pseudo fruit) develops from ovary + other floral parts like thalamus (e.g., apple, strawberry, cashew). The edible part of apple is primarily thalamus tissue.

**Dehiscent fruit types:** Legume (opens along two sutures, e.g., pea), follicle (opens along one suture, e.g., Calotropis), capsule (opens in various ways, e.g., cotton, mustard), silique (long fruit with false septum, e.g., mustard), caryopsis (indehiscent, grain-like, e.g., wheat — fruit and seed fused).

**Floral whorls and their fertility:** The four whorls are (from outermost to innermost): calyx (sterile, protective), corolla (sterile, attractant), androecium (male, fertile — produces pollen), gynoecium (female, fertile — produces ovules). Flowers with all four whorls are 'complete'; missing one or more are 'incomplete'.

**Meristem types in stems:** Apical meristem (tip growth), intercalary meristem (node/base, e.g., grasses), lateral meristem (cambium — secondary growth). Monocots generally lack lateral meristem (no secondary growth), while most dicots have it.

**Economic importance of selected families:** Brassicaceae — mustard, cabbage, broccoli, radish, turnip (vegetables, oilseeds). Fabaceae — pulses (gram, arhar, urad), oilseeds (soyabean, groundnut), fodder (berseem), nitrogen fixation. Solanaceae — potato (food), tomato (food), tobacco (drug), brinjal (food), ornamentals (Petunia). Liliaceae — onion, garlic (vegetables), aloe (medicine), tulip (ornamental), vanilla (flavouring).

**Angiosperm diversity:** Over 300,000 species in ~300 families. Largest families: Asteraceae (~25,000 spp.), Orchidaceae (~22,000 spp.), Rubiaceae (~14,000 spp.), Fabaceae (~14,000 spp.), Poaceae (~12,000 spp.). Monocots: ~60,000 spp. in ~60 families.
confusion: Tetradynamous stamens (Brassicaceae) means 6 stamens total: 4 LONG + 2 SHORT. Do not confuse with '4+2' arrangement — it is specifically 4 long outer stamens and 2 short inner stamens.
Papilionaceous corolla (Fabaceae) has 5 petals arranged as: 1 large UPPER (banner/vexillum) + 2 LATERAL (wings) + 2 LOWER fused (keel). This is different from a regular 5-petaled flower.

Pome fruit (apple) is NOT a true berry — it is a pseudo Fruit because the fleshy part is derived from the thalamus (receptacle), not just the ovary wall. True berry (banana, tomato) develops entirely from ovary.

In epigynous flowers (e.g., sunflower, apple), the ovary is INFERIOR — the floral parts attach ABOVE the ovary. In hypogynous flowers (e.g., mustard), the ovary is SUPERIOR — floral parts attach BELOW the ovary.
Monochlamydeae (Bentham & Hooker) does NOT mean 'no perianth' — it means perianth is absent OR the calyx and corolla are indistinguishable (both look like tepals, e.g., Liliaceae).

APG system does NOT use traditional family/order/class ranks in the same way. It is a phylogenetic cladogram based on DNA, not a ranked Linnaean system. Modern classification increasingly follows APG.

A silique (Brassicaceae fruit) is NOT the same as a legume (Fabaceae fruit). Silique has a false septum and opens by two valves; legume opens along two sutures (ventral and dorsal) with seeds on both margins.

Double fertilisation in angiosperms involves TWO fusion events (syngamy + triple fusion) producing TWO products (zygote + endosperm). Gymnosperms have only ONE fusion event (sperm + egg) and NO endosperm formation by fertilisation — their nutritive tissue is the pre-existing female gametophyte (n).

Parallel venation does NOT mean veins are perfectly parallel — they run roughly parallel but may have connecting veins (e.g., in Curcuma). Reticulate venation has a net-like pattern with prominent midrib and branching veins.

universalFacts: Angiosperms are the most diverse group of land plants with over 300,000 described species, representing approximately 90% of all plant species.

Double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms — one sperm fuses with the egg (forming zygote 2n), the other fuses with two polar nuclei (forming triploid endosperm 3n). This is energetically efficient.
The transition from gymnosperm to angiosperm is one of the most significant evolutionary events in plant history, occurring around 130–200 million years ago (early Cretaceous).
Over 75% of global food crops are angiosperms. The three most important crops — rice, wheat, and maize — are all monocot angiosperms.
Bentham and Hooker's classification (1862–1883) was the first comprehensive natural system for angiosperms and was used in Indian botanical surveys for over a century.
The Asteraceae (sunflower) family is the largest family of angiosperms with about 25,000 species. They share a unique capitulum inflorescence with two types of florets.
Orchidaceae seeds are the smallest of any plant — a single orchid pod can contain up to 50,000 dust-like seeds, each with an embryo consisting of just a few cells.
The water transport efficiency of angiosperm xylem (with vessel elements) is 10–100 times greater than that of gymnosperm xylem (tracheids only), enabling faster growth rates.
